question: Should I Hire a Fractional CRO If My VP of Sales Just Quit?
body:
## Direct Answer If your VP of Sales just quit, hiring a fractional CRO is often the right move for the next three to nine months — it buys you senior go-to-market leadership in weeks instead of the six-plus months a full-time executive search typically takes, stabilizes the pipeline and the team while you decide what you actually need, and costs a fraction of a loaded C-level salary. Treat it as a deliberate bridge with a defined mandate and exit criteria, not a permanent replacement, and it will usually pay for itself in retained pipeline and avoided panic-hiring. The moment a VP of Sales resigns, most founders and CEOs feel two competing urges at once: replace the role immediately so the number doesn't fall off a cliff, and freeze so they don't repeat whatever hiring mistake led here. A fractional Chief Revenue Officer sits precisely in the gap between those two urges. This essay walks through when a fractional CRO is the correct response to a VP departure, when it isn't, how the economics compare to the alternatives, what the engagement should actually deliver, and how to structure it so you end up with a stronger revenue org — not just a warm body in a Zoom square. ## What is a fractional CRO and how is it different from the VP of Sales you just lost? A fractional CRO is an experienced revenue executive who works with your company part-time — commonly one to three days a week — on a fixed-term or rolling contract rather than as a full-time employee. The "chief revenue officer" scope matters here: a CRO owns the entire revenue engine, which usually spans sales, sales development, revenue operations, and often the commercial handoffs with marketing and customer success. That is deliberately broader than a VP of Sales, who typically owns the sales team and quota attainment but not the surrounding system. This distinction is the whole reason the fractional route can be more than a like-for-like patch. When a VP of Sales quits, the instinct is to backfill the same box on the org chart. But a departure is also a rare, low-cost moment to ask a bigger question: was the pipeline actually being managed as a system, or was one person heroically carrying it? A seasoned fractional CRO diagnoses the revenue architecture — segmentation, ICP, pipeline coverage ratios, forecast hygiene, comp design, the RevOps stack — not just the headcount gap. They've usually run this play across many companies, so pattern recognition is their core asset. Where a VP is embedded and operational, a fractional leader is deliberately senior, external, and time-boxed, which changes both what you get and how you should use them. If you want to go deeper on how revenue operations underpins all of this, see [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-operating-model](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-operating-model). The trade-off is presence. A fractional CRO is not in every standup, will not personally coach every rep through every deal, and cannot substitute for day-to-day frontline sales management if that's what's actually broken. Understanding that boundary up front is what separates a successful bridge engagement from an expensive consulting relationship that never quite lands. ## When should a VP of Sales departure trigger a fractional CRO hire? Not every resignation calls for a fractional executive, so the honest first step is to classify the situation. A fractional CRO is a strong fit when the departure has created a genuine leadership vacuum at a company that still has real revenue to protect, and where a rushed full-time hire is the biggest risk in the room. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[VP of Sales just quit] --> B{Is there an active book of pipeline at risk right now?} B -->|No, pre-revenue / very early| C[Founder-led sales + a coach
fractional CRO likely premature] B -->|Yes, real pipeline| D{Do you know exactly what next VP profile you need?} D -->|Yes, clear profile| E{Can you close a great full-time hire in under 90 days?} D -->|No, unsure of the gap| F[Fractional CRO to diagnose + bridge] E -->|Yes| G[Interim IC coverage + fast search
fractional optional] E -->|No, 4-9 mo search| F F --> H[Define mandate, exit criteria,
and knowledge-transfer plan] H --> I{Diagnosis says system is sound?} I -->|Yes| J[Hire permanent VP,
fractional exits] I -->|No, structural gaps| K[Fractional stays as CRO
or rebuilds before VP hire] ``` The clearest positive signals: you're a company somewhere between roughly Series A and Series C (or a bootstrapped equivalent with several million in revenue) where the number genuinely matters this quarter; the VP's departure leaves nobody senior who can own forecasting and deal strategy; you don't yet have a crisp picture of the profile your next full-time leader should have; and a proper executive search will realistically take four to nine months. In that combination, the cost of leaving the seat empty — slipping deals, a demoralized team, a forecast nobody trusts — dwarfs the cost of the fractional engagement. The negative signals matter just as much. If you're pre-revenue or very early and the founder is still the best salesperson in the building, a fractional CRO is usually premature — what you need is founder-led selling plus targeted coaching. If the real problem was one bad hire on top of a healthy system, you may only need short-term IC-level coverage and a fast search. And if the departure exposed that your economics simply don't support a repeatable sales motion yet, no revenue leader — fractional or full-time — will fix a product or pricing problem. Diagnose honestly before you spend. For the framing on whether your motion is even ready to scale, [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/pipeline-coverage-ratio](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/pipeline-coverage-ratio) is a useful gut check. ## What does hiring a fractional CRO actually cost versus the alternatives? The economics are the argument that usually wins the room, but only if you compare the right things. A full-time CRO or senior VP of Sales is one of the most expensive hires a growth-stage company makes: base salary, an on-target variable component, equity, benefits, and the fully loaded overhead on top. Ranges vary widely by market, stage, and geography, so you should price your own market rather than trust any single number — but the structural point holds regardless of the exact figures. Compare on total cost of the *decision*, not just the monthly invoice. A fractional engagement is billed for a slice of a week, so its cash cost is materially lower than a full-time loaded package, and it carries no severance, equity dilution, or long-term commitment. Against that, weigh the two costs that founders routinely under-count. First, the cost of a vacant seat: every week the forecast drifts, reps freelance their own process, and your best people quietly update their own résumés. Second — and this is the big one — the cost of a bad full-time hire made in a hurry. A senior revenue leader who doesn't work out typically isn't discovered for two or three quarters, and by then you've lost the ramp time, the comp, the opportunity cost, and often several good reps who left under them. The fractional bridge exists largely to let you avoid making that expensive mistake under duress. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Panic["Panic full-time hire"] P1[Fast search, pressure] --> P2[Loaded C-level cost] P2 --> P3{Right fit?} P3 -->|Miss ~2-3 qtrs later| P4[Sunk comp + lost ramp
+ rep attrition + redo search] P3 -->|Hit| P5[Good outcome] end subgraph Bridge["Fractional bridge"] B1[Fractional CRO in weeks] --> B2[Part-time cost,
no severance/equity] B2 --> B3[Stabilize + diagnose] B3 --> B4[Hire the right VP
with a real scorecard] B4 --> B5[Warm handoff] end ``` There's a second economic benefit that's easy to miss: a good fractional CRO makes the *eventual* full-time hire cheaper and more likely to succeed. Because they've mapped your revenue engine, they can write the real scorecard for the permanent role, help you interview for it, and hand off a documented operating system instead of a mess. You're effectively paying for a diagnosis and a de-risked search on top of the interim coverage. That combined return is why the fractional path so often beats both "leave it empty" and "hire fast" on a pure cost-of-decision basis. RevOps tooling and reporting discipline are a big part of what makes that handoff clean — see [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/forecast-hygiene](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/forecast-hygiene). ## What should you expect a fractional CRO to deliver in the first 90 days? An engagement without a mandate becomes an expensive advisory retainer, so the single most important thing you do is define outcomes and a timeline before day one. The first 90 days should follow a recognizable arc: stabilize, diagnose, then rebuild or hand off. Compress or extend the phases to your situation, but keep the sequence. In the first two to three weeks — the stabilize phase — the priority is stopping the bleeding. That means personally touching the deals that are actually at risk, reassuring the team that there's a steady hand on the wheel, cleaning up the forecast so leadership can trust the number again, and making sure no critical customer or partner relationship falls through the cracks left by the departure. Nothing structural gets rebuilt yet; the goal is simply that the quarter doesn't collapse while the diagnosis happens. The diagnose phase, roughly weeks three through six, is where the fractional CRO earns their premium. Expect a clear-eyed assessment of the whole revenue system: is the ICP and segmentation right, is pipeline coverage adequate, is the sales process real or theatrical, is comp aligned to the behavior you want, is RevOps giving you trustworthy data, and — crucially — was the VP who left a symptom or a cause? This is where you learn whether you have a people gap or an architecture gap, and that answer determines everything downstream. The final phase, weeks six through twelve, splits based on the diagnosis. If the system is fundamentally sound and you just need the right permanent leader, the fractional CRO helps you define the role, source and vet candidates, and prepare a clean handoff. If the diagnosis surfaced structural problems — broken comp, no pipeline discipline, a stack that can't report reality — then rebuilding those foundations *before* you hire a permanent VP is the higher-value use of the engagement, because you don't want to hand a new leader the same broken system that contributed to the last departure. Either way, insist that knowledge is documented and transferable, not locked in the fractional's head. Deliverables you should expect in writing include a revenue operating cadence, a forecasting methodology, a comp-plan review, and a scorecard for the permanent hire. ## How do you structure the engagement so it strengthens the org instead of creating a new dependency? The biggest failure mode of any fractional or interim leadership arrangement is that it quietly becomes permanent by inertia — the "temporary" leader is still there a year later, the team now routes everything through them, and you've recreated single-point-of-failure risk with less accountability and no equity alignment. Avoiding that is a matter of structure, and you set it at the start. Start with explicit exit criteria written into the agreement. The engagement should end when specific conditions are met — a permanent leader is hired and ramped, or a defined set of foundations is rebuilt and documented — not on a vague "we'll see how it goes." Pair that with a defined cadence for reviewing progress against those criteria, so drift gets caught early. A rolling monthly contract with clear checkpoints is usually healthier than either a one-week trial (too short to deliver anything structural) or a locked twelve-month commitment (removes the pressure to actually transition out). Insist on knowledge transfer as a first-class deliverable, not an afterthought. Everything the fractional CRO builds — the operating cadence, the forecast model, the deal-review format, the comp logic, the reporting — should live in shared documents and systems that survive their departure. A useful test: if the fractional leader vanished tomorrow, could your team run the revenue motion from what's written down? If the answer is no, they're building dependency, not capability. Guard against the related trap where the fractional leader hoards the key relationships; part of their job is to distribute account and partner relationships across your team so nothing collapses when they leave. Finally, protect the team dynamics. Be transparent with the sales org about what the arrangement is and isn't — an experienced hand steadying the ship and helping choose the next permanent leader — so people don't spend the quarter speculating about their future instead of selling. Give the fractional CRO real authority during the engagement (they can't stabilize a team they can't actually direct), but make clear internally that the goal is a durable, well-run revenue org that stands on its own. Done this way, the departure of your VP becomes the moment your revenue engine got professionalized rather than the moment it wobbled. For more on building durable revenue operating systems, [https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/sales-comp-design](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/sales-comp-design) covers the comp foundations most departures expose. ## What are the risks and red flags to watch for? A fractional CRO is a tool, and like any tool it can be misapplied, so it's worth naming the ways this goes wrong. The most common is treating the fractional leader as a permanent solution and never running the search — the bridge becomes the destination, and you've traded one form of key-person risk for another while paying premium rates indefinitely. The second is hiring a fractional who is a strategist but not an operator, when what your bleeding pipeline actually needs is someone willing to get into deals; a beautiful strategy deck does not close the quarter. Watch, too, for the mismatch between scope and reality. A part-time leader genuinely cannot substitute for full-time frontline sales management if the core problem is that your reps need daily coaching and accountability — in that case you may need interim IC-level or manager-level coverage alongside, or instead of, the CRO. Be wary of any fractional who resists documentation, keeps relationships and knowledge to themselves, or can't articulate clear exit criteria; those are the tells of someone optimizing for engagement length rather than your outcome. And be honest that a fractional CRO cannot fix a product-market-fit or unit-economics problem masquerading as a sales-leadership problem. Vet for pattern-matched experience at your stage and motion specifically — someone who has scaled enterprise sales may be the wrong fit for a high-velocity SMB motion, and vice versa. The right structure and the right person turn a scary departure into an upgrade; the wrong ones just move the risk around. ## Related questions ### How quickly can a fractional CRO start compared to a full-time hire? Typically within one to three weeks, versus roughly four to nine months for a full-time executive search including sourcing, interviewing, offer, notice period, and ramp. Speed of coverage is one of the main reasons to choose the fractional route after a sudden departure. ### Can a fractional CRO also help hire my permanent VP of Sales? Yes — one of the highest-value outputs is a real scorecard for the permanent role, plus help sourcing, interviewing, and vetting candidates against the actual gaps they diagnosed. A clean handoff to the eventual full-time leader is a core deliverable, not a bonus. ### Is a fractional CRO the same as an interim or contract VP of Sales? Not quite. A CRO scope spans the whole revenue engine — sales, SDRs, RevOps, and commercial handoffs — while an interim VP of Sales typically covers just the sales team. Choose based on whether your gap is systemic or contained to frontline sales management. ### What company stage is a fractional CRO right for? Most commonly growth-stage companies with real revenue to protect — roughly Series A through C or a bootstrapped equivalent — where a vacant leadership seat is costly but a rushed full-time hire is the bigger risk. Pre-revenue companies usually need founder-led selling and coaching instead. ### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last? Usually three to nine months, structured on a rolling basis with explicit exit criteria and regular checkpoints. It should end when a permanent leader is hired and ramped, or when defined foundations are rebuilt and documented — not drift into a permanent arrangement by inertia. ## FAQ **Should I tell my sales team the CRO is fractional?** Yes. Transparency prevents a quarter of anxious speculation. Frame it accurately: an experienced leader steadying the ship and helping choose the next permanent VP, with real authority during the engagement. Ambiguity breeds attrition faster than an honest interim arrangement does. **Will a fractional CRO actually get into deals or just advise?** The good ones do both, and in the stabilize phase they personally touch at-risk deals. If a candidate positions themselves as purely strategic and won't engage operationally, that's a red flag for a post-departure bridge, where hands-on deal work is exactly what protects the quarter. **How is a fractional CRO priced?** Typically as a fee for a set number of days per week on a fixed-term or rolling contract, with no equity, severance, or full benefits load. Price your own market rather than trusting a single benchmark, and compare on total cost of the decision — including the cost of a vacant seat and a bad rushed hire — not just the monthly invoice. **What if the diagnosis says my whole revenue system is broken, not just the missing VP?** Then the higher-value use of the engagement is rebuilding those foundations — comp, pipeline discipline, forecasting, the RevOps stack — *before* you hire a permanent leader, so you don't hand a new VP the same broken system that contributed to the last departure. That's the fractional CRO earning their fee. **Can I use a fractional CRO permanently instead of hiring full-time?** Some very small or capital-efficient companies do run on fractional leadership for extended periods, but for most growth-stage companies it's a bridge. The risk of "permanent by inertia" is real: you recreate key-person risk with less accountability and no equity alignment. Set exit criteria up front regardless. **What deliverables should I insist on in writing?** A revenue operating cadence, a forecasting methodology, a comp-plan review, documented deal-review formats, and a scorecard for the permanent hire. The test: if the fractional leader vanished tomorrow, could your team run the motion from what's written down? If not, they're building dependency instead of capability. **Does a fractional CRO replace my RevOps function?** No — they lead and often improve it, but a CRO owns the revenue strategy and system while RevOps executes the operations, data, and tooling underneath it. A strong fractional CRO will actually strengthen your RevOps discipline as part of stabilizing the forecast and reporting. **What if I can't afford even a fractional CRO right now?** Then scope down honestly: short-term IC or manager-level interim coverage plus a fast search may be enough if the underlying system was healthy and the VP was the only gap. A fractional CRO is most justified when the departure exposed uncertainty about what you actually need, not merely an empty seat. ## Sources - [Harvard Business Review — Sales Leadership and Go-to-Market](https://hbr.org/topic/subject/sales) - [First Round Review — Building and Scaling Revenue Teams](https://review.firstround.com/) - [SaaStr — Sales Leadership, Fractional Executives, and CRO Guidance](https://www.saastr.com/) - [Harvard Business Review — Onboarding and Executive Transitions](https://hbr.org/2017/03/how-to-onboard-new-hires-at-every-level) - [Bessemer Venture Partners — Scaling Go-to-Market](https://www.bvp.com/atlas) - [OpenView Partners — SaaS Metrics and Sales Efficiency](https://openviewpartners.com/blog/) - [McKinsey & Company — Growth, Marketing & Sales Insights](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/growth-marketing-and-sales/our-insights) - [Gartner — Sales and Revenue Leadership Research](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales) ## Related on PULSE - [The RevOps Operating Model](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-operating-model) - [Pipeline Coverage Ratio Explained](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/pipeline-coverage-ratio) - [Forecast Hygiene Fundamentals](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/forecast-hygiene) - [Designing Sales Comp Plans That Retain Reps](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/sales-comp-design)
